thread.title: Utilities: Timely? Sector Comments Plus 3 Stocks To Consider - Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLU)

author: DoctoRx
title: Utilities: Timely? Sector Comments Plus 3 Stocks To Consider - Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLU)
text:
Introduction - Bucking Conventional Wisdom on Utilities With one major exception - NextEra Energy ( NEE ) - I agree with consensus that regulated electric and gas utility stocks in the US should generally be treated as bond proxies and thus should not have especially high P/Es. Based on that, with the 10-year Treasury note in the 2.9-3.0% range, my observation is that most utility stocks ( XLU ), and the large XLU ETF itself, are not great sources of alpha relative to the long-term potential of the S&P 500 ( SPY ). However, XLU is a good trading vehicle, some of the utilities in it appeal to me as sources of alpha as buy-and-hold investments, and there are substantial defensive characteristics from almost all members of XLU.
This article covers two topics, one that XLU could be an interesting trade here in that investors may rotate toward safety in the stock market, and the other a discussion of NEE and two utilities that have underperformed XLU substantially over the past half year or so.
In mostly thinking of XLU as largely a trading sardine, I'm doing so in the spirit of looking for alpha, not criticizing at as a part of a permanent portfolio interested in income and safety.
In searching for alpha , I am a buy-and-hold investor in Apple ( AAPL ) and many other companies that do not have their upside capped by regulators, that are in growth parts of the economy, that may have net cash as AAPL and some other companies do, and that in many cases have lower P/Es than XLU, which per its SPDR web page has a forward P/E of 16.1X and a current yield around 3.48%.
However, over the very long run, ownership of an ongoing basic and essential business such as a utility should outperform fixed income, and I'm not definitely in love with utility bonds. Once I get longer than 10 years in maturity, the yields on utility bonds look clearly less attractive to me than ownership of the stocks.
Now, with all those details clarified (I hope), first up, here's why I think that XLU may have attractive technicals both for traders and for long-term investors looking for a potentially reasonable entry point.
Looks Like the Opposite of Two Years Ago By May-June of 2016, prolonged periods of low energy prices and low interest rates had accompanied weak economies.
The stage was therefore set for renewed growth.
And indeed, XLU was strong and reached $52.95 by mid-2016 versus $50.50 today. However, by this January and continuing into later this spring, instead of input prices having dropped sharply and for a prolonged period as was the case by May-June 2016, they had risen sharply and for a prolonged period (not just oil and interest rates, also labor in some sectors). This is the opposite of the set-up in mid-to-late 2016, and thus my interest in new money investments is much less aggressive now than it was then. As in 2016, when markets only took off after the US election, this sort of trend shift tends to be a process that occurs over time. As an example, I've been shifting my commentaries in this less exuberant direction beginning, as it happens, around the time the SPY peaked this year:
On Jan. 25, I wrote a cautionary article where some of the Summary bullet points read as follows:
The pro-business actions of Donald Trump have been thoroughly recognized by traders, but two future negatives may have been ignored. These negatives are the Fed's hostile stance, and the potential for declining profit margins, which are at very high levels per S&P. Having provided a successful list of cyclical stock choices last August, I now argue for caution on many of them. SPY was then at 2,842 versus 2,721 at last Friday's close. Full disclosure: I was bearish on Netflix ( NFLX ) in the article though not advocating a short position, and it has surged since then. But overall, NFLX aside a modified risk-off point of view, i.e. taking lots of profits in late January in tech (not AAPL, though) and in financials, sticking to value, not buying bonds or interest-sensitive stocks for alpha , and having lots of cash on the sidelines, has worked pretty well this year.
Now I think that the odds in favor of defensive stocks beating the averages have increased. I also have been propounding domestic over international investments, and see a good deal more turmoil ex-US than domestically, so I am sticking to that theme. Utilities meet both criteria.
In the next section, two charts help make a case for a non-recessionary - though possibly temporary - change of leadership.
Two Charts Favoring Playing More Defense The first chart shows how extreme the positioning of speculators has gotten. They are collectively confident that having more than doubled from their 2016 record low, yields on the 10-year Treasury are set to go higher. This is shown by the record or near-record net positioning of commercial hedgers (mostly, dealers, I believe) as shown by the green line far above the zero line in the bottom panel of the following FINVIZ chart of the price of the bond on the futures market:
(For a closer look at recent periods, click on the "D" or "W" tab on the top right of the linked web page.)
In general, high levels of commercial hedgers being net long the bond - easily seen even on this multi-decade chart - have correlated with subsequent rising prices for the bond, i.e. falling interest rates. This is today's situation and by analogy is technically bullish for bond prices, i.e. favors declining interest rates on the long end of the yield curve.
A close look at the counter-trend falling interest rate periods in early 2004, and again in much of 2005, shows that the bond-bearish speculators were heavily negative then - and wrong; the hedgers were correct when they were net long the bond. Post-Great Recession, the same correlations are clear in the long-term bond bullish period from Q2 2010 into 2016, and again briefly in early 2017, when rates surprisingly began dropping into the fall.
So that's one previously reliable pattern. We shall see if it works again.
Remember also that positioning can change quickly. No technical indicator can simply be taken "to the bank."
The second chart shows the 5-year performance (price only, not total return) of SPY, XLU and the Vanguard ETF (NYSEARCA: EDV ) that owns volatile, long-term zero coupon Treasuries:
XLU data by YCharts
The Goldilocks period came during QE 3 in 2014 when there was so much liquidity around that everything could go up in price - and except for inflation hedges, that's what happened. Then came a period, beginning in early 2015, where both utilities and bonds outperformed stocks. Then, with the Fed finally tightening and reversing QE (shrinking liquidity) came a more normal situation: stocks went up but bonds down in price (interest rates up), and eventually utilities dropped in price with bonds (This was what was considered a normal bull market all the way from 1982 to 2007, before the distortions associated with QE).
Does another reversal of fortune loom?
XLU has gone nowhere for two years while other stocks have soared, and long-term bonds have given a negative total return in that period. International crises are again featured on the Bloomberg News bond page , which often correlates with good relative strength in defensive, domestic stocks, such as utilities.
Some readers may wish to consider the possibility.
Moving along, some observations on individual utility stocks that I like based on valuation at current prices. All are southeastern utilities, where good growth prospects meet up with generally constructive regulation. All names are large caps with diversified operations. What follows are some capsule comments.
NextEra Energy, Aptly Named This is to a large extent, a green, growth-oriented utility play.
NEE comprises FPL (Florida Power & Light), a Florida electricity producer and distributor that is #1 in the US by retail MWh sales (see slide 3 of the May 2018 presentation ) and NextEra Energy Resources , a large producer of renewable energy. NEE has been on a roll, and trades as a growth stock. It recently announced a major acquisition of several Florida properties from Southern Company ( SO ). Regulatory approvals will take some time to be obtained.
NEE is also planning on a late-2018 completion of the acquisition of the Vero Beach electric system. More deals will likely follow in due course. ( Could JEA be in NEE's sights ?)
FPL is a low-cost, reliable producer of electricity, and is an innovator in several ways. This has led to what Slide 10 shows, namely that FPL is a outlier in a good way in operational cost effectiveness. This in turn allows it to do deals as discussed above with positive results.
The other part of NEE is NEER, aka Energy Resources as NEE calls it, the renewable energy subsidiary. NEER also manages natural gas pipelines in Texas, but its main activities are production of energy from wind. NEER has significant growth plans; see the 2018 presentation and the materials from the Q1 earnings report for more details.
Exposure to NEER can be gained via a small-cap stock, NextEra Energy Partners ( NEP ). This is an LP that sends a 1099 form .
I am not certain now NEP will react if crude oil prices drop significantly, as I have suggested was a very reasonable possibility. I have an unrealized gain in NEP, but with the recent downside action in crude oil, I may sell it Tuesday. I've never followed it previously and probably should observe how it trades under different market and economic conditions.
NEER has $42 B in total assets and generated $5.2 B in revenues in 2017 (Slide 13).
I like NEE for the long term even at Friday's close of $162.42 and look at it as trading at about 16X EPS based on about $10 EPS to be earned, it is hoped, in 2021. The current dividend yield of 2.75% is "low" because the Street agrees that this is a growth company, thus it values NEE as a growth stock. I concur and think it can and will provide modest alpha over the long haul with above-average predictability and consistency of growth. I do not think there is any end in sight to growth either of Florida or of renewable energy production, thus of all higher-P/E utilities, NEE is the one I think is best positioned for investors at current valuations.
Next, two large utilities that have underperformed XLU.
Duke Energy ( DUK ) - Big and Arguably Undervalued This $53 B market cap company, headquartered in fast-growing North Carolina but also operating in South Carolina and Florida (and elsewhere), may be a strong stock to buy now; at least, I'm hoping that's the case.
DUK closed at $75.81 Friday, way down from its November peak of $91.80. The dividend yield is 4.70%. Consensus EPS (likely adjusted, not GAAP) is $4.95 next year and $5.19 in 2020.
Morningstar's May 18 write-up of DUK suggests a fair value estimate of $87. I do not see a lot of major pitfalls in the offing here (see next section for one of them, though). But the market is smart, and certainly DUK has not dropped in a vacuum, so I'm taking nothing for granted.
DUK may have more snapback potential in the months ahead than NEE has appreciation potential, given that NEE is near its all-time high. Perhaps DUK has simply overreacted to the bond rout and could retrace a lot of its move down from last fall's high.
Dominion Energy ( D ) - Controversial, but I Like It This name has been viewed until recently as a safe stock, but several issues have arisen. These include, without limitation:
A delay in construction of at least part of the Atlantic Coast Pipeline, which it shares with DUK and SO, surprise financial issues with Dominion Midstream Partners ( DM ), a pipeline and LNG company, and the proposed takeover of SCANA ( SCG ), which has significant nuclear-related uncertainties. D has fallen from a December high of $85 to $64.17. The dividend yield is 5.2%. Management insists this dividend will be increased at a healthy pace for the next 1-2 years, and then at a slower pace thereafter. Obviously some traders disagree.
Morningstar's May 18 write-up of D estimated fair value at $84. It is unclear if this incorporates the May 15 Appeals Court decision adverse to D, DUK and SO about the AC; it could not have incorporated D's follow-up commentary that the great majority of construction could continue as of now.
Too much is in flux with D to bother discussing consensus estimates.
My general view translates to the specific to D: most of these situations work out for the modestly brave investor who buys a generally high-quality asset.
Trading in D could get even more interesting, and I'm going to try to watch D with a Z en point of view.
Risks All investments have risk, and so does XLU, though presumably the risk is more in the range of price drop of the ETF exceeding dividend payouts. NEE, DUK, D and all individual utilities have similar risks, and as we see with SCG and other utilities today and historically, a utility is a business that has all sorts of business risks. A greater degree of safety is gained from a bond. So, all investors in my view need to be alert to a degree of risk from utility stocks.
Concluding, and Macro, Comments As I have been arguing in a contrarian manner since late January, the Fed's tightening program has been more aggressive than many pundits have been saying. Even the current Bond King, Jeff Gundlach, has been quite the bull on gold ( GLD ) and quite the bear on his specialty of bonds. Yet the reversal of QE, with the Fed shrinking its balance sheet as well as hiking short-term rates, is unprecedented - and continues on pace in an accelerating tightening fashion. This tightening of both the price and quantity of money may explain why despite upside surprises to corporate earnings and growth this year, SPY is virtually flat and is down from late January, when the sugar high from tax cuts was maximal. Previously, as in 1981, Fed tightening has tamed inflation faster than expected, and defensive assets have gained ground.
The prime rate will go to 5.0% if and when the Fed raises rates again the week after next when the FOMC meets; 5% is a historically normal level.
Thus the US is no longer in a crazy low interest rate environment as it was a few years ago. The US government actually has the highest borrowing costs of any of the old British group of countries/colonies, namely the UK itself, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. So there is some room for long rates here to drift lower even with the Fed raising short rates, i.e. more yield curve flattening (the old Greenspan conundrum; see 2004-5 above).
In the setting of good economic growth and steady long-term rates which could move in any direction or no direction at all, with gold back under $300/ounce and oil for the moment off the boil, with speculators and many experts alike seemingly all in on further carnage in bond-land, I'm interested in some all-weather income-oriented assets again such as XLU represents.
My own preference over XLU these days is for individual names, which carry no management fee and which lack certain other risks that ETFs have. Having sold out of my prior utility favorite WEC Energy ( WEC ) at its recent spike above $64 recently for a very nice gain (entry point around $56 in late November 2016), I'm happier with NEE over WEC. I see NEE as offering faster, cleaner and more diversified growth at a roughly similar P/E. I also see DUK and D for extra income with perhaps similar growth as WEC offers. In other words, I'm going with the uptrend in NEE and buying the dips in DUK and D, understanding there are risks with all of them. I'll revisit these trades as appropriate.
To be clear, again, most electric or electric and gas utilities in the US are more similar than differentiated, so I'm not especially arguing with the mythical Mr. Market here about all the others; in fact, as a retiree, I own two utilities for income but not alpha , Con Ed ( ED ) and American Electric Power ( AEP ). Thus I'm comfortable bringing XLU to your attention, along with NEE, DUK and D as individual names.
Thanks for reading and sharing any thoughts you wish to contribute.
Disclosure: I am/we are long NEE, D, DUK, AEP, ED, NEP, AAPL, IEF.
